touches.text: INTENTION:
The ticket owns its refusals: a gate refuses a crossing on the ticket's behalf. The gates are CodeMother's (9.3.5).
Coding Ticket: what we usually mean.
ground_loop (machine): the heartbeat
It launches each device's cairn/devices/<device>/groundloop/pulse.py, each as its own process (5.8.3.4).
It writes one JSON record at the end of a pass listing each device: beat time, device folder found or NOT FOUND, file mtime, pid spawned. It does no checks and no takeover.
Owns the inspectors and gates (9.4): everything in the code pipeline that checks. The exception is diagnostic_inspector, which is base's (17.1).

Outline check: when a ticket is cast, the cheapest model reads it beside the outline sections it touches. A conflict, or an open question in those sections, becomes a [Q#n] at the outline line it bears on (0.6.2), and that open [Q#n] holds the ticket's build until it is answered. It reads the outline as it stands each time, so editing the outline costs nothing. WHY: a ticket that contradicts the outline builds something Akien did not intend, and the cheapest time to catch that is before the build. - CC
tester
PURPOSE: The system's notary: runs proofs and seals their verdicts.

WHY: Law 8: nothing enters proven-space without a proof a hollow build couldn't pass, and the verdict must come from a hand the builder did not guide. A green cannot be self-granted. A machine under CodeMother, not a device: CodeMother does not build, so the tester inside her puts no builder between a build and its verdict, and nothing here needs its own process in the rack, since each proof run is its own process already.
INTENTION:
Runs a proof as its own process and writes a validation record (claim, caller, date, method, verdict, evidence, falsifier, horizon).
Hollow runs: proves a proof goes red when the build is removed.
A tooth whose live subject was deleted retires with it, when fixture teeth still cover the behaviour.
Seals: one current validation per proof, beside the proof. A seal holds while the code it measured is unchanged.

A seal is host independent: one record per proof, whichever box asks. Seals are made by one sealing machine in the cairn device, and there is only ever one cairn (until a laptop dies and a backup takes over), so there is one sealer. A box that is not cairn's home asks the sealer instead of writing its own seal.
A timed-out run is its own outcome, not red.
A proof that cannot go red without its build (its hollow is empty) stands only on Akien's answered approval, recorded as the hollow reading and re-read at clearance; any other empty hollow is red.
TOOLS: base, validation_store, proof_coverage, scratch, question, proof_discovery, chain, bus_client, artifact, system_word; machine build_inspector; db client.
VERBS: run, notices, CodeMother's verbs reached over the bus (RULE 1). COMMANDS: cairn codemother test (--hollow, --seal, --exec, ...), shortcut cairn test; proofgate (the hook: proofs run by hand).
build_inspector

Once build_inspector moves into CodeMother, code outside her reaches it over the bus: the 18 crossing calls in transitions.py, the other code sites and the 82 proofs that run a sieve over themselves. No published client tool, no fifth exception: that is what the bus is for.

artifact: the one door a record of truth changes through, and the journal of who came through it (hash-chained, caller read from the kernel). WHY: errors are permanent in records of truth (Law 7), and the journal is what shows a record moved by hand. USERS: everyone who writes a record.
scratch: a proof's throwaway temp dirs and worktrees, cleaned up by the door. WHY: a run must leave nothing behind (4.3.1.7). USERS: the tester.
validation_store: reads and writes seals. USERS: the tester.

RULE 1, ENCAPSULATION: every component talks to every other only through that component's public interface: a device's is the bus plus any client tool it publishes; a machine's or tool's is what its entry declares. Nothing outside a device reaches into its code, skills included. A ticket builds inside its own component, and its proofs measure only that component. WHY: it limits a change to the component that made it.

THE SYSTEM LEARNS ITS GATES: each gate holds a confidence with its provenance, moved by derivation and by experience. A miss moves it more than a pass; silence is weak evidence. A gate whose act is irreversible or outward facing has a ceiling below its threshold, so it always asks. Thresholds are per gate; when derivation and experience disagree, the gate asks Akien. "How does this learn?" is asked of every component.
Test runs are transient (30 days, 4.3.2); seals are records of truth (git).

Commit: the proofs of the component the ticket changed, since RULE 1 bounds a change to its component. Passing them puts the component in service, yellow: proven where it changed, not yet measured against what depends on it. In service needs only the best we can do now: 80% trust.

Reds don't get lost. Each run writes a ticket for every new red it finds and every orphaned file it sees, unless one is already open for it. A red seen in passing gets the same treatment. Every red and every orphaned file is fixed; one unrelated to the work in hand is ticketed, and once it is, that crossing can go ahead.

A line states the intention (the build target) in plain words: what it is and why. Every new input, answered question or measurement is read for how it changes or elaborates an intention or a why. That meaning is folded in; the words and the history that carried it are left out. Why? Because when we left the history in, it was much easier to get lost in THE SPECIFICS OF WHAT WAS SAID rather than what was meant. Whys are used when ajudicating conflicts at the level before asking the operator.

The abstract ticket owns what every kind shares: its birth (cast) and its three parts, each with one job: the plan (only what a builder builds from), the metadata and state (what gates and doors read and write as it moves), and the history (the append-only log). WHY: one job per part reduces confusion; a builder reads the plan and nothing else.

The ticket IS its own manager. It carries its workflow and status, and asks each gate whether it can transit. If refused, it gets itself back to design for fixing. If no handler is available to ask, it throws a trouble and waits until we decide. Design is CC and Akien until the outline is implemented; a design agent comes after that. Until then a refused ticket waits in the trouble lane, which both read when a session opens, and nothing posts to a design verb that no machine answers.

A ticket's code is a tool or machine; its life is data. All of its state is on disk, so anyone can instantiate it to talk to it, and any dialog is written to the relevant part of the ticket as it happens. To cross a gate the ticket asks that gate to queue it, sending only its fileref: devices/codemother/0/machines/<inspector>/queueme <fileref>. The gate instantiates the ticket from that fileref on its own side. A ticket instance then processes the pass or fail: on a pass it goes on to the next step, alerting the probes watching the gate (3.3.4.2); on a fail it asks design to queue it, the same way. Self-queuing is the abstract ticket's (3.3.2), so every kind inherits it and no caller queues a ticket on its behalf. WHY: encapsulation. The ticket crosses as a fileref and the other side builds its own instance, so nothing is shared across the boundary but the address.
Weekly: what is too long or too host-bound to run daily, such as hollow re-runs of every proof and each box's own run of the proofs it can run.

A red is first a question: is the code wrong, or is the tooth measuring the wrong thing? An LLM reads the work against the component's why, the tooth's why and CP1-CP6, because even the Laws rest finally on the core principles. Either the code or the tooth changes, and a tooth change carries that decision in the same act (corrosion, 17.11.6). A tooth a hollow build could pass is worthless at every tier (Law 8).

conflicts.text: A seal is host independent: one record per proof, whichever box asks. Seals are made by one sealing machine in the cairn device, and there is only ever one cairn (until a laptop dies and a backup takes over), so there is one sealer. A box that is not cairn's home asks the sealer instead of writing its own seal.
conflicts.ticket_says: evidence['hollow_anchor'][tid]['not_run'] records which teeth this specific host could not run (printed UNRAN) and carries this host-specific information in the seal
conflicts.why: 9.4.2.3.3.1 states 'A seal is host independent: one record per proof, whichever box asks.' The ticket makes the seal's contents differ by host—a Windows seal will record different not_run_teeth than a Linux seal for the same proof. This violates the clause 'whichever box asks' should get the same record. The seal is no longer host-independent; different hosts will produce different seal records with different host-specific not_run_teeth arrays.

conflicts.text: A proof that cannot go red without its build (its hollow is empty) stands only on Akien's answered approval, recorded as the hollow reading and re-read at clearance; any other empty hollow is red.
conflicts.ticket_says: When every declared tooth of a proof is not run on this host, raise HollowUnmeasurable naming the proof, the teeth, and 'not run on this host.' This outcome is not red.
conflicts.why: The outline states 'any other empty hollow is red.' A hollow where all declared teeth are unrun on this host is empty (no teeth green) and would be an 'other' empty hollow under the outline's logic, triggering automatic red. The ticket instead raises HollowUnmeasurable, which is not red. Both outcomes cannot hold for the same situation.
